content: Two typhoid vaccines are currently available in the United States. The first is an oral live, attenuated vaccine known as the Vivotif Berna vaccine, which is derived from the Ty21a strain of Salmonella Typhi and manufactured by the Swiss Serum and Vaccine Institute. The second is an intramuscular Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (ViCPS), marketed as Typhim Vi and produced by Sanofi Pasteur. Both vaccines provide protection to approximately 50% to 80% of recipients. An older intramuscular heat-phenol-inactivated vaccine, previously manufactured by Wyeth-Ayerst, was discontinued in 2000. Combined hepatitis A and typhoid fever vaccines are not approved for use in the United States, though they may be available in other countries. The primary vaccination schedule differs between the two vaccines. For the oral Ty21a vaccine, the regimen consists of four capsules, taken every other day. These capsules must be refrigerated (but not frozen) and consumed with cool liquid (not exceeding 37°C or 98.6°F) approximately one hour before a meal. The manufacturer advises against administering Ty21a to children under six years of age. For the ViCPS vaccine, primary vaccination involves a single 0.5 mL (25 µg) dose administered intramuscularly. The manufacturer does not recommend this vaccine for children under two years of age. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions to these vaccines are documented, but there is limited information regarding their safety during pregnancy. As a precaution, it is generally advised to avoid vaccinating pregnant women. The live, attenuated Ty21a vaccine is contraindicated in immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV, due to theoretical safety concerns. For these individuals, the intramuscular ViCPS vaccine is considered a safer alternative. The only contraindication for the ViCPS vaccine is a history of severe local or systemic reactions to a previous dose. Neither vaccine should be administered to individuals experiencing an acute febrile illness. Precautions and Contraindications The live Ty21a vaccine may have reduced immunogenicity in individuals concurrently receiving antibiotics, immune globulin, or certain viral vaccines. Laboratory studies have shown that the growth of the live Ty21a strain is inhibited by various antibacterial agents. Therefore, vaccination with Ty21a should be delayed for at least 24 hours after the administration of any antibacterial medication. However, available data suggest that simultaneous administration of oral polio or yellow fever vaccines does not reduce the immunogenicity of Ty21a. If typhoid vaccination is deemed necessary, it should not be delayed due to the administration of viral vaccines. Additionally, co-administration of Ty21a with immune globulin does not appear to pose any significant issues. What is Typhoid? Typhoid fever is a serious illness caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi. It is characterized by high fever, weakness, abdominal pain, headache, loss of appetite, and occasionally a rash. If untreated, typhoid fever can be fatal in up to 30% of cases. Some individuals who recover from typhoid may become asymptomatic carriers, capable of transmitting the disease to others. The primary mode of transmission is through the consumption of contaminated food or water. While typhoid is rare in the United States, most cases occur in individuals who have traveled to regions where the disease is endemic. Globally, typhoid affects approximately 21 million people annually and causes around 200,000 deaths. Vaccination can help prevent typhoid fever. Typhoid Vaccines Two types of typhoid vaccines are available: an inactivated (killed) vaccine administered as an injection and a live, attenuated (weakened) vaccine taken orally. Who Should Receive the Typhoid Vaccine? Routine typhoid vaccination is not recommended in the United States. However, it is advised for: Travelers to regions where typhoid is prevalent (note that the vaccine is not 100% effective and does not replace the need for careful food and water precautions). Individuals in close contact with a typhoid carrier. Laboratory personnel who work with Salmonella Typhi. Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection) Not recommended for children under two years of age. A single dose provides protection and should be administered at least two weeks before travel to allow the vaccine to take effect. A booster dose is required every two years for individuals who remain at risk. Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral) Not recommended for children under six years of age. Four doses are required, taken two days apart. A booster dose is needed every five years for individuals who remain at risk. Both vaccines can be administered concurrently with other vaccines. Who Should Not Receive the Typhoid Vaccine? Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection) Individuals who have experienced a severe reaction to a previous dose should not receive another dose. Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral) Individuals who have had a severe reaction to a previous dose should not receive another dose. Immunocompromised individuals should not receive the live vaccine and should instead opt for the inactivated vaccine. This includes individuals with: HIV/AIDS or other conditions affecting the immune system. Prolonged use of immunosuppressive medications, such as corticosteroids. Cancer or those undergoing cancer treatments, including chemotherapy or radiation therapy. The oral vaccine should not be administered within 24 hours of certain antibiotics. Consult a healthcare provider for more information. Risks Associated with Typhoid Vaccines As with any medical intervention, typhoid vaccines carry a small risk of adverse effects, including severe allergic reactions. However, the likelihood of serious harm or death from these vaccines is extremely low. Severe complications are exceedingly rare. Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection) Mild reactions may include: Fever (occurs in approximately 1% of recipients). Headache (occurs in approximately 3% of recipients). Redness or swelling at the injection site (occurs in approximately 7% of recipients). Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral) Mild reactions may include: Fever or headache (occurs in approximately 5% of recipients). Abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or rash (rare). What to Do in Case of a Moderate or Severe Reaction Signs to Watch For: Unusual symptoms, such as high fever or behavioral changes. Signs of a severe allergic reaction, including difficulty breathing, hoarseness, wheezing, hives, pallor, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. Steps to Take: Seek immediate medical attention. Inform the healthcare provider about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. Report the reaction to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) by contacting a healthcare provider, visiting the VAERS website (www.vaers.org), or calling 1-800-822-7967. Additional Information For further details, consult a healthcare provider, contact your local or state health department, or reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) at 1-800-232-2522 (English) or 1-800-232-0233 (Español). Additional resources are available on the CDC’s typhoid website.
